item.title: Alleged Israeli spy company heavily targeted Starlink users, sources say
item.description: Experts at a digital defense firm recently found that an Israeli ad tech company was heavily targeting users of Starlink's satellite internet service in a likely effort to spy on them, according to six people familiar with the matter.
item.dc:creator: Raphael Satter
item.content:encoded: Experts at a digital defense firm recently found that an Israeli ad tech company was heavily targeting users of Starlink's satellite internet service in a likely effort to spy on them, according to six people familiar with the matter. Researchers at TrendAI, a unit of Tokyo-based cybersecurity company Trend Micro (4704.T) , concluded the Israeli company Discover-Tech was one of the biggest sources of digital ads shown to users of SpaceX's Starlink service and that the ads were likely being used to geolocate or otherwise surveil them, according to the six people. The researchers, who drew on digital advertising data in TrendAI's telemetry for their conclusions, found that Discover-Tech had become one of the world’s leading bidders for ads aimed at Starlink users and that it was the No. 1 bidder on Starlink traffic in more than 100 countries, including several where Starlink itself was banned or restricted. Bidding refers to the complex auction system by which advertisers secure space inside people's browsers and apps. SpaceX (SPCX.O) did not respond to requests for comment. Discover-Tech and its chief executive did not respond to requests for comment over the past two weeks. TrendAI released a report on October 15 about the targeting of Starlink users but did not name Discover-Tech, instead saying the party responsible was “an ad tech entity” which it called “Shadow-Earth-79.” The six sources said Shadow-Earth-79 is TrendAI’s codename for Discover-Tech. TrendAI did not directly address questions about why its report did not identify Shadow-Earth-79 by name, saying in a statement that its approach to attribution was aimed at reducing the risk of mistakes and avoiding "hype-driven labels" or "unstable actor names that can mislead defenders, distort risk prioritization, and trigger inappropriate response actions." Finding ways to track Starlink users has become a cottage industry as governments around the world try to get a grip on the spread of satellite internet terminals. Because they route data through SpaceX-operated satellites rather than nationally regulated telecommunications firms, the terminals can sidestep local internet restrictions, communicate in hostile areas or coordinate action across battlefields. Starlink has become [USN:L5N46A00R TEXT:"a particularly important resource"] in Ukraine, whose military relies on the service [USN:L8N46213X TEXT:"for frontline communications"] and [USN:L8N4350JH TEXT:"directing drone strikes"]. In May, Israeli newspaper Haaretz and the website Intelligence Online separately reported that Israeli-owned businesses were pitching clients on ways to identify and track Starlink users. Haaretz said exploiting ad data appeared to play a key role in the process. DISCOVER-TECH ACCUSED OF WIDER SPY EFFORT The same day that TrendAI published its report on Shadow-Earth-79, Canadian cyber watchdog Citizen Lab and New York advertising technology firm Confiant [USN:L6N45Z04V TEXT:"outed Discover-Tech by name"]. Both groups said the Israeli company abused the ad bidding process, which can leak data about internet users back to the bidder. Over time, bidders can collect that leaked data, collate it and merge it with other information to de-anonymize users, follow them around the web and, in some cases, set them up for targeting with surveillance software. Citizen Lab and Confiant said the ads had been shown inside dozens of sensitive networks belonging to media organizations, governments and tech firms . In response to the investigations, Google, Comcast and other companies said they had removed Discover-Tech from their ad platforms. At least one big US tech company and one international organization recently launched internal inquiries into whether Discover-Tech's ads targeted their employees, according to one of the people and a seventh person familiar with the matter. TOP ADVERTISER IN YEMEN, SOUTH SUDAN TrendAI's report cited suspicious bidding patterns that suggested Shadow-Earth-79 was running "targeting and tracking infrastructure rather than a commercial advertising operation." In addition to noting the "obvious skew" towards buying ads aimed at Starlink users, the report said that Shadow-Earth-79 was the top buyer of ads in Syria, Libya, Yemen and South Sudan and was the No. 2 ad buyer in Afghanistan even though "the demand for legitimate Western advertising in sanctioned or active-conflict states is effectively zero." It said the entity won "an implausibly dominant share" of bids in several countries including Hungary, Israel, Egypt, Azerbaijan and Venezuela. TrendAI researchers were convinced Discover-Tech was behind the suspicious bidding activity and discussed naming the company in TrendAI's report, according to the six people familiar with the matter. But they eventually dropped the idea of publicly attributing the activity to a named company after TrendAI executives raised legal concerns, five of the sources said. Self-censorship is common in the cybersecurity industry, especially when executives fear that exposing surveillance operations could draw retribution, industry experts say. Earlier this year, US cybersecurity company Palo Alto stripped explicit references to China from a report on a global cyberespionage campaign even though its researchers were confident the hacking could be pinned on Beijing, [USN:L6N3Z714C TEXT:"Reuters reported at the time"]. Reuters said the report was watered down over fears that calling out China would cause problems for Palo Alto's operations there, which were already under scrutiny following a Beijing directive ordering domestic companies [USN:L1N3YF0B5 TEXT:"not to use its products"]. Palo Alto said the lack of attribution in its report was not correlated with "procurement regulations in China" and that any suggestion otherwise was "speculative and false."

item.title: Jailed Tanzanian opposition leader starts hunger strike
item.description: Tanzanian opposition leader Tundu Lissu, who was charged with treason last year, has started a hunger strike to protest his inability to access his lawyers, his party said.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Tanzanian opposition leader Tundu Lissu, who was charged with treason last year, has started a hunger strike to protest his inability to access his lawyers, his party said. Lissu, who leads the CHADEMA opposition party and came second in the 2020 presidential election, began refusing food on Monday after his lawyers were denied entry to the prison where he is being held, party spokesperson Brenda Rupia wrote on X. Tanzania Prisons Service spokesperson Elizabeth Mbezi said in a statement that Lissu was not on a hunger strike and was safe, and that the prisons service continued to allow his lawyers to see him "after being satisfied that they are his advocates and nothing else". Lissu was charged with treason over what prosecutors said was a speech calling on the public to rebel and disrupt last year's general election. He pleaded not guilty to the charges, which his lawyer has said are politically motivated. Tanzania's electoral commission had barred CHADEMA from participating in the polls after it failed to sign a code of conduct document. The election was marred by protests and unrest, with a government-appointed commission of inquiry saying the [USN:L6N4160ZJ TEXT:"violence that broke out"] afterwards led to at least 518 deaths and blaming the protesters for the violence. CHADEMA's chief legal counsel, Rugemeleza Nshala, told journalists on Saturday that Lissu had planned the strike because he was denied privacy during talks with his lawyers in violation of a court order. The court is due to deliver its judgement in Lissu's case on November 6. Lissu's detention, along with the alleged abductions of government critics, has shone a spotlight on the human rights record of President Samia Suluhu Hassan, who won the 2025 election. The government has rejected accusations of widespread rights abuses and said it is committed to respecting human rights. It ordered an investigation into reports of abductions in 2024, though no official findings have been made public.

item.title: Israeli exit polls show deadlock, point to setback for Netanyahu
item.description: Israel's wartime election appeared deadlocked on Tuesday, exit polls showed, with Gadi Eisenkot's opposition bloc running neck and neck with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's camp, leaving neither side with a clear path to power.
item.dc:creator: Maayan Lubell, Lili Bayer, Tamar Beeri
item.content:encoded: Israel's wartime election appeared deadlocked on Tuesday, exit polls showed, with Gadi Eisenkot's opposition bloc running neck and neck with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's camp, leaving neither side with a clear path to power. The projections pointed to a setback for Netanyahu's coalition and potentially weeks of political wrangling to form a government, though the deadlock could allow Israel's longest-serving prime minister to remain in power as caretaker during coalition negotiations. "We must establish a strong, right-wing government," Netanyahu told Likud party supporters after 3 a.m. (0100 GMT) during a speech in Jerusalem, highlighting Israel's military successes and what he described as a historic opportunity to "remove the Iranian threat." Kan 11 and Channel 13 showed the two blocs level, while Channel 12 showed Netanyahu's Likud-led camp taking a narrow edge over Eisenkot as the night progressed. None gave either side the 61 seats needed for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. "The Israeli public has voted against Netanyahu's service as Israel's prime minister ... a worthy leader would have accepted the people's non-confidence and announced today his retirement from politics," Eisenkot earlier told cheering supporters in Tel Aviv. Far-right religious parties led by Itamar Ben-Gvir and Bezalel Smotrich were projected to take a combined 13 seats within Netanyahu's bloc. Arab parties outside the two main blocs could hold the balance of power. But Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party and a former military chief, has all but ruled out forming a government with them, complicating his path to power. Voter turnout was 77.7%, Israel's Central Elections Committee said, the highest in more than two decades and around 7 percentage points higher than in 2022. Final results could take days, and Israel's fragmented political system leaves smaller parties potential kingmakers in coalition negotiations that have run to weeks or months after past elections. If neither bloc can form a government, another vote may need to be held, something Eisenkot opposed. "In an election with such a high turnout it would be a mistake to go to another election," he said. Tuesday's vote was the first election since the Hamas-led attack of October 7, 2023, and the ensuing wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. Yohanan Plesner, president of the Israel Democracy Institute, called the exit polls a major defeat for Netanyahu's coalition but cautioned that Eisenkot had not emerged as a clear winner and much could change as votes were counted. NETANYAHU SETBACK, NO CLEAR WINNER Opposition leader Yair Lapid said in a statement: “Don’t let anyone confuse you: the Netanyahu bloc has suffered a crushing defeat. This is a total collapse and the public has told them to go home.” Eisenkot, 66, who lost a son and two nephews in the Gaza war, emerged as Netanyahu's strongest challenger, stressing his security credentials while positioning himself as a centrist domestically. He entered politics only four years ago and joined Netanyahu's war cabinet after the 2023 Hamas attack, but quit eight months later, criticising the prime minister's leadership. [USN:L6N46303T TEXT:"Eisenkot offers a break"] with Netanyahu's leadership and far-right allies, but not with the hawkish approach to security that has become more entrenched since the 2023 Hamas attack. He opposes Palestinian statehood and says Hamas' military wing must be destroyed or dismantled. Eisenkot says Israel's response — a war that has killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, according to Gaza health authorities — was a failure because Hamas remains in charge. He told Israel's defence establishment that Netanyahu had lost the people's faith and warned the prime minister not to subject Israel's security to his own political interests. The headquarters of the Joint List, an alliance of several Arab parties, burst into whistles and applause when exit polls were released, on a historic night for turnout among Palestinian citizens of Israel. “We refuse the occupation and racism, and we will remain here,” said Faten Gattas, a candidate in the Joint List, in a speech at the alliance’s headquarters in Nazareth. Candidates hoped high Arab turnout would allow them to play a decisive role in blocking Netanyahu's coalition from returning to power. A WARTIME VERDICT Voters grappled with the trauma of Israel's deadliest day, when Hamas killed 1,200 people and took 251 hostage, and the wars in Gaza and with Lebanon's Hezbollah and Iran that followed. While Netanyahu was criticised for the country's biggest security failure, he argued that he had made Israel and the world safer by killing top leaders of Hamas, Hezbollah and Iran. The policies of Netanyahu's right-wing coalition have been divisive at home and deepened Israel's international isolation, but he has portrayed himself as the leader with the mettle to face down Israel's foes. Netanyahu, 77, has served as prime minister for nearly 19 of the past 30 years and has repeatedly survived political crises. His opponents have managed to wrest the premiership from him only once since 2009, after four inconclusive elections in two years. Eighteen months later, he was back. He entered the election facing long-standing corruption charges, which he denies, and criticism over intelligence failures that allowed Hamas-led militants to carry out their attack.

item.title: Republicans bet Musk’s millions can rescue Texas' Paxton in US Senate race
item.description: Texas Democrats' best chance at a statewide win in more than three decades is facing a wall of Republican money, with Elon Musk and other donors pouring hundreds of millions into a late effort to rescue Senate candidate Ken Paxton.
item.dc:creator: Brad Brooks, Andy Sullivan, Arathy Somasekhar
item.content:encoded: Texas Democrats' best chance at a statewide win in more than three decades is facing a wall of Republican money, with Elon Musk and other donors pouring hundreds of millions into a late effort to rescue Senate candidate Ken Paxton. With two weeks until the November 3 election and early voting under way, however, it is unclear how much impact the spending can still have. Polls show few undecided voters remain, and Republicans say their biggest challenge is turning out their own voters, many of whom are frustrated by the cost of living and the war with Iran launched by President Donald Trump, who has endorsed Paxton. "The money being spent now isn't for persuasion. It's for mobilization," said pollster James Henson, director of the Texas Politics Project at the University of Texas. "In most of the statewide polling we've seen, Republicans are suffering from an enthusiasm gap." Republican strategists say internal polling shows that gap has narrowed considerably. "We've seen it collapse, thank God. It was one of our concerns," said Dave Carney, a longtime Republican strategist and chief adviser to Texas Governor Greg Abbott. That turnout challenge helps explain the tone of Republican advertising. Rather than focusing on inflation and the economy, which polls consistently show are among voters' top concerns, Republicans in Texas and other battleground states have leaned heavily on culture-war themes to energize their base. Republican groups have spent more than $100 million nationally since August 1 on more than 200 ads accusing Democrats of backing “sex change” procedures for children, according to an analysis of AdImpact data by FactCheck.org. TEXAS-SIZED SPENDING Combined advertising spending in the race between Paxton, the state's Republican attorney general, and Democrat James Talarico has topped $500 million, according to ad-tracking data, putting it on pace to become the most expensive US Senate contest ever. Talarico has held a small but consistent lead over Paxton, though generally within the margin of error, making it Texas' most competitive statewide race since 1994, Henson said. Outside groups backing Paxton have spent about $239 million, more than five times the roughly $45 million spent by the largest Democratic-aligned groups. Texas PAC, a Republican super PAC, alone has accounted for nearly $149 million. The group was launched by the Senate Leadership Fund, the main Republican Senate super PAC. Musk, who lives in Texas and has relocated SpaceX, Tesla, X and other businesses there, has contributed $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, which subsequently transferred matching sums to Texas PAC, according to federal filings. Talarico has offset the outside-spending disadvantage with grassroots fundraising. His campaign says it raised $64 million from July through September, more than triple Paxton's total, with 97% of donations under $100. He spent $61 million on ads through September, according to AdImpact, while the biggest Democratic outside group, Lone Star Rising PAC, has spent $19.3 million. The influx of Republican money arrived relatively late in the campaign, with Trump's MAGA Inc. super PAC not beginning major spending until early September. "I think the cavalry arrived just in the nick of time for Paxton," said Republican donor and oil businessman Dan Eberhart. GOING NEGATIVE Much of that spending has funded attacks portraying Talarico as out of step with Texas voters on culture-war issues. Independent fact checkers say the ads distort Talarico's record, and Henson said their goal is “arousing negative sentiment among Republican voters” to boost turnout. Texas PAC ads tell voters that Talarico is "for they/them, not you" and accuse him of supporting taxpayer-funded sex-change surgeries for minors. PolitiFact rated that claim false, noting that while Talarico opposed a 2023 ban on gender-transition care for minors, he has said he opposes gender-reassignment surgery for children. A Paxton campaign ad featured an AI-generated Talarico reading from a fictional "King James (Talarico) Bible" that combined excerpts of his past remarks, including one describing God as "nonbinary." FactCheck.org said the ad lacked key context. Talarico has responded by casting Paxton as "the most corrupt politician in Texas." Paxton was impeached by the Republican-controlled Texas House in 2023 on abuse-of-office allegations but was acquitted by the state Senate. Separate state securities-fraud charges dating to 2015 were dropped in 2024 under an agreement requiring community service, ethics training and restitution. Paxton denied wrongdoing. The Paxton campaign did not respond to requests for comment. It has previously said Talarico raises the allegations to distract from his own record. Some voters say the Republican attacks are unconvincing. Sal Anthony Rodriguez, a 32-year-old Houston operations manager who voted for Trump in 2020 and 2024, said he now supports Talarico, partly because of what he views as misleading attacks. "I've seen a lot of ads saying that he is in 100% support for transgender surgeries on kids, and a quick Google search showed that that was not accurate," Rodriguez said. Democrats argue the focus on cultural issues reflects Republican difficulty addressing voters' economic concerns. "Voters are really pissed off about the state of their lives right now, and you can only run so many trans ads at people who are sick of paying $6 for diesel," said Chuck Rocha, a senior adviser to the Talarico campaign.

item.title: In the wake of Reliance Jio's listing, what are India's biggest share offerings?
item.description: Jio Platforms became India's second-largest company by market capitalisation after its shares soared 21% in their record Mumbai debut on Wednesday, giving Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Industries its first listing in two decades.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Jio Platforms (JIOP.NS) became India's second-largest company by market capitalisation after its shares soared 21% in their record Mumbai debut on Wednesday, giving Mukesh Ambani's Reliance Industries its first listing in two decades. [USN:L2N46E033 TEXT:"Shares of the company,"] whose main business is telecoms, opened at 1,358 rupees a share, compared with its 1,119-rupee offer price. Jio is now valued at about $131.52 billion, overtaking Bharti Airtel and HDFC Bank. Here are the five largest Indian IPOs before Jio: NATIONAL STOCK EXCHANGE The National Stock Exchange (NSEI.BO) became one of the world's 10 most valuable publicly traded bourses last month, with a market capitalisation of about $48 billion, after a [USN:L4N4590D5 TEXT:"$2.3 billion market debut"]. The stock listed at 1,800 rupees on the BSE on September 24, up 0.84% from its issue price of 1,785 rupees. HYUNDAI MOTOR INDIA Hyundai (HYUN.NS) , the world's third-largest automaker and India's fourth-biggest passenger vehicle maker, raised 278.7 billion rupees ($2.93 billion) in October 2024 in what is currently India's second-biggest IPO, after Jio. The manufacturer's South Korean parent (005380.KS) sold a 17.5% stake in a pure offer for sale, where existing shareholders sell shares and no new capital is raised. LIFE INSURANCE CORPORATION OF INDIA The government pocketed roughly 205 billion Indian rupees ($2.16 billion) from selling a 3.5% stake in India's largest insurer and biggest domestic financial investor (LIFI.NS) , a far cry from its initial target of up to $12 billion. The shares slid nearly 8% on their debut. PAYTM [USN:L1N2S906S TEXT:"Paytm"] (PAYT.NS) , an Indian fintech firm, raised 183 billion rupees ($1.92 billion) in November 2021 in a mix of a fresh share issuance and an offer for sale. Ant Group reduced its stake to 23% from 28% and SoftBank's Vision Fund pared its holding to 16%. Paytm lost more than 27% on its debut, the biggest listing-day drop in Indian IPO history at the time. TATA CAPITAL The Tata Group's financial services arm (TATC.NS) raised 155 billion rupees ($1.63 billion) in October 2025, with Tata Sons and IFC among those selling in the offer-for-sale component alongside a fresh issue. The IPO was the largest ever by a non-banking financial company in India. The shares [USN:L3N3VU09S TEXT:"listed"] at a slight premium of 1.23%. ($1 = 95.1150 Indian rupees)
